key_evidence.fact: Intravenous pyelogram shows multiple cysts in the collecting ducts of the medulla with no obstruction
key_evidence.why: Cystic dilation of the medullary collecting ducts (the 'sponge' appearance) is the pathognomonic imaging finding of medullary sponge kidney and directly distinguishes it from stone disease or obstruction.

key_evidence.fact: Recurrent urinary tract infections over the past few years
key_evidence.why: Stasis within the dilated medullary cysts predisposes to recurrent UTIs, a hallmark of medullary sponge kidney that is not typical of simple nephrolithiasis or uncomplicated hematuria.

key_evidence.fact: Visible blood in the urine with right flank pain and no recent trauma
key_evidence.why: Gross hematuria with flank pain reflects cyst-related bleeding/stone passage in the medullary sponge kidney, and the absence of trauma argues against renal contusion.

key_evidence.fact: Positive right costovertebral angle tenderness with mild-to-moderate right flank tenderness and no palpable mass
key_evidence.why: Localized renal tenderness without a mass supports an intrinsic medullary/collecting system process rather than a tumor or large obstructing lesion.

key_evidence.fact: Urinalysis shows too-numerous-to-count RBCs with negative nitrites and normal creatinine/BUN
key_evidence.why: Marked hematuria without nitrite-positive infection and preserved renal function points to a structural medullary cause rather than pyelonephritis or renal failure.

confusable.distinguishing: Stones cause colicky flank pain with obstruction/hydronephrosis on imaging, whereas medullary sponge kidney shows medullary collecting-duct cysts without obstruction.
Pyelonephritis presents with fever, dysuria, and nitrite-positive urine; this patient is afebrile with negative nitrites and cystic medullary imaging.
ADPKD shows multiple large cortical and medullary cysts with enlarged kidneys and often renal impairment/family history, unlike the small collecting-duct cysts confined to the medulla here.

key_evidence.fact: The patient reports discomfort and pelvic floor muscle tension during attempted vaginal penetration.
key_evidence.why: Pain and involuntary pelvic floor tension with penetration are the defining features of genitopelvic pain disorder and distinguish it from painless sexual dysfunction.

key_evidence.fact: The initial attempt at speculum examination was aborted due to the patient's pelvic floor muscles tensing up and discomfort.
key_evidence.why: Objective reproduction of pain and pelvic floor guarding on examination confirms the diagnosis rather than a purely psychological or unexplained complaint.

key_evidence.fact: External genitalia are normal appearing with no redness, and there is no vaginal discharge.
key_evidence.why: Absence of inflammatory, infectious, or dermatologic findings excludes vulvovaginitis and other local causes of dyspareunia.

key_evidence.fact: Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterus and adnexa with no fibroids or ovarian cysts.
key_evidence.why: Normal pelvic imaging excludes structural causes such as endometriosis, fibroids, or adnexal pathology that can mimic pelvic pain.

key_evidence.fact: Hormonal profile including FSH, LH, estradiol, progesterone, and testosterone is normal.
key_evidence.why: Normal hormonal testing rules out endocrine causes of dyspareunia and infertility such as hypoestrogenism or androgen excess.

confusable.disease: Vaginismus (now classified under genitopelvic pain/penetration disorder)
confusable.distinguishing: Vaginismus is characterized predominantly by involuntary muscle spasm preventing penetration, whereas this case includes both pain and pelvic floor tension, fitting genitopelvic pain disorder.
Infectious causes would show discharge, erythema, or abnormal wet mount; here the vulva is normal with no discharge.
Endometriosis typically causes cyclic pelvic pain and abnormal imaging findings; this patient has normal ultrasound and no structural lesions.

key_evidence.fact: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive with positive HBeAg and HBc IgG, indicating ongoing viral replication and chronic infection
key_evidence.why: HBsAg positivity beyond 6 months with HBeAg indicates active chronic HBV, distinguishing it from acute self-limited hepatitis or resolved infection (anti-HBs positive).

key_evidence.fact: Markedly elevated transaminases with AST 488 U/L and ALT 798 U/L (ALT > AST)
key_evidence.why: Hepatocellular pattern with ALT predominance reflects active hepatic inflammation typical of chronic hepatitis B flares, unlike the cholestatic pattern of biliary disease or the AST>ALT pattern of alcohol-related injury.

key_evidence.fact: Mild scleral icterus with dark urine and direct hyperbilirubinemia (total 3.6, direct 2.4 mg/dL)
key_evidence.why: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with jaundice confirms hepatobiliary injury and supports active hepatitis rather than a purely constitutional illness.

key_evidence.fact: Tender hepatomegaly palpated 2-3 cm below the right costal margin
key_evidence.why: A tender enlarged liver points to acute-on-chronic hepatic inflammation, discriminating from painless hepatomegaly of infiltrative or malignant disease.

key_evidence.fact: History of consuming regional foods at a state fair over a month ago
key_evidence.why: This exposure raises suspicion for hepatitis A (positive IgG here reflects past exposure/immunity), helping differentiate co-existing or prior HAV from the active HBV driving the current illness.

confusable.distinguishing: HAV IgM would be positive in acute infection; here only HAV IgG is positive (past exposure/immunity), while HBsAg/HBeAg positivity indicates HBV as the active cause.
Alcohol-related injury typically shows AST:ALT ratio >2 with GGT elevation; this case shows ALT predominant over AST and positive HBV serology, pointing to viral rather than alcohol etiology.
Acute HBV would show IgM anti-HBc; the presence of IgG anti-HBc with HBsAg and HBeAg indicates chronic infection with active replication rather than a recent acute acquisition.

key_evidence.fact: Sudden onset of severe periumbilical abdominal pain that is out of proportion to the mild tenderness found on palpation
key_evidence.why: Pain out of proportion to exam findings is the classic hallmark of acute mesenteric ischemia and distinguishes it from peritonitis or uncomplicated gastroenteritis.

key_evidence.fact: Recent hospitalization for acute myocardial infarction one week ago
key_evidence.why: Recent MI is a major embolic risk factor for superior mesenteric artery occlusion, strongly linking the abdominal presentation to mesenteric ischemia rather than a primary GI cause.

key_evidence.fact: Epigastric bruit heard on auscultation
key_evidence.why: An epigastric bruit suggests mesenteric arterial stenosis/occlusion and is a discriminative physical finding pointing to a vascular cause of abdominal pain.

key_evidence.fact: Bloody loose bowel movements in the setting of acute abdominal pain
key_evidence.why: Bloody stools indicate mucosal ischemia/infarction of the bowel, supporting mesenteric ischemia over functional or inflammatory bowel disease.

key_evidence.fact: CT angiography showing reduced blood flow to the mesenteric arteries
key_evidence.why: CTA demonstrating compromised mesenteric arterial perfusion is the definitive diagnostic evidence confirming acute mesenteric ischemia.

confusable.distinguishing: Pancreatitis typically causes pain with elevated lipase/amylase and marked epigastric tenderness, without bloody diarrhea or a mesenteric bruit, and CTA would not show mesenteric arterial occlusion.

Peritonitis produces rigid, guarding abdomen with rebound tenderness and free air on imaging, whereas mesenteric ischemia classically shows pain out of proportion to mild tenderness without pneumoperitoneum.

Colitis usually has diarrhea with fever and inflammatory changes confined to the colon; mesenteric ischemia shows pain out of proportion, vascular risk factors, epigastric bruit, and CTA evidence of reduced mesenteric arterial flow.

key_evidence.fact: Episodic cough and shortness of breath that worsen with exertion (climbing stairs) and at night
key_evidence.why: Nocturnal and exertional worsening of episodic respiratory symptoms is a hallmark of variable airway obstruction in asthma, distinguishing it from fixed obstruction like COPD.

key_evidence.fact: Diffuse end-expiratory wheezes on auscultation
key_evidence.why: Diffuse expiratory wheezing reflects reversible bronchospasm and supports asthma over parenchymal or cardiac causes of dyspnea.

key_evidence.fact: Spirometry showing FEV1/FVC ratio of 65% with reduced FEV1 (60%), indicating obstructive ventilatory defect
key_evidence.why: An obstructive spirometric pattern confirms airflow limitation, and in this episodic clinical context it points to asthma rather than restriction or normal lungs.

key_evidence.fact: Onset of symptoms following an upper respiratory tract infection 8 weeks ago (fever, sore throat, nasal congestion)
key_evidence.why: A viral URI is a classic trigger for new or worsened asthma, helping distinguish it from other chronic causes of cough and dyspnea.

key_evidence.fact: Normal chest X-ray with no focal abnormalities
key_evidence.why: A normal chest radiograph excludes pneumonia, mass, or other structural disease, supporting a functional/reversible airway diagnosis like asthma.

confusable.distinguishing: COPD typically has fixed, progressive obstruction in an older heavy smoker without episodic nocturnal variability; here the episodic, exertion/night-predominant symptoms and post-viral onset favor asthma.
Post-viral cough usually resolves and lacks documented obstructive spirometry and diffuse wheezing; the persistent obstructive defect and wheeze point to asthma.
Heart failure would show orthopnea, crackles, edema, or cardiomegaly on imaging; this patient has a normal chest X-ray, no crackles, and no chest pain or palpitations.

key_evidence.fact: High fever of 40.5°C (104.9°F) that resolved, followed 5 days later by a rash that began on the trunk and spread to the extremities
key_evidence.why: The classic roseola pattern of a rash appearing after defervescence of a high fever distinguishes it from measles and rubella, where the rash typically accompanies or follows the fever differently.

key_evidence.fact: Maculopapular rash that blanches on pressure and is nonpruritic
key_evidence.why: A blanching maculopapular rash supports a viral exanthem like roseola and argues against petechial/purpuric processes such as meningococcemia.

key_evidence.fact: Posterior auricular lymphadenopathy present
key_evidence.why: Posterior auricular/occipital lymphadenopathy is characteristic of roseola and helps differentiate it from measles (which has Koplik spots and prominent cough/coryza/conjunctivitis).

key_evidence.fact: A 1-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure during the high fever in a previously healthy infant with up-to-date immunizations
key_evidence.why: A brief febrile seizure during high fever is a recognized complication of roseola and, in an otherwise well-immunized infant, points away from meningitis/encephalitis as the cause.

key_evidence.fact: Infant is currently afebrile and well-appearing with no irritability or feeding difficulties
key_evidence.why: A well-appearing infant after defervescence with a rash supports a benign viral exanthem like roseola rather than a serious bacterial infection or invasive disease.

confusable.distinguishing: Measles typically has fever concurrent with the rash plus cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots; roseola rash appears after fever resolution without these catarrhal features.
Rubella rash usually starts on the face and spreads downward with tender posterior cervical/suboccipital nodes and low-grade fever, whereas roseola follows a very high fever and starts on the trunk.
Meningococcemia causes non-blanching petechial/purpuric lesions and an ill-appearing child, unlike the blanching maculopapular rash and well appearance in roseola.

key_evidence.fact: Skin biopsy shows intraepidermal accumulation of edematous fluid and widening of intercellular spaces between keratinocytes (spongiosis)
key_evidence.why: Spongiosis is the histologic hallmark of eczematous dermatitis and distinguishes it from psoriasis (acanthosis with parakeratosis) and lichen planus (band-like lymphocytic infiltrate).

key_evidence.fact: Pruritic (itchy) rash is the dominant symptom
key_evidence.why: Intense pruritus is characteristic of eczematous dermatitis, whereas psoriasis is often only mildly itchy and tinea may itch less prominently.

key_evidence.fact: Chronic course lasting 5 months with intermittent flares but never complete resolution
key_evidence.why: A relapsing chronic course fits eczematous dermatitis; acute contact dermatitis or drug eruption would typically resolve after trigger removal, and tinea would not persist unchanged for months without treatment.

key_evidence.fact: Erythematous, scaly, crusted, slightly raised rough lesions without warmth or induration
key_evidence.why: Scaly crusted plaques without warmth/induration support an eczematous process rather than cellulitis (warm, tender, indurated) or an acute urticarial eruption.

key_evidence.fact: No new medications, no new substances/contact exposures, and no recent illness
key_evidence.why: Absence of an identifiable exogenous trigger or preceding illness argues against allergic contact dermatitis or a viral/post-infectious exanthem and supports endogenous eczematous dermatitis.

confusable.distinguishing: Psoriasis shows well-demarcated silvery plaques with Auspitz sign and histology of acanthosis, parakeratosis, and Munro microabscesses rather than spongiosis; itch is usually milder.
Tinea has an annular lesion with central clearing and an active scaly border; KOH prep shows fungal hyphae, and biopsy would not show spongiotic dermatitis.
Contact dermatitis is temporally linked to a specific exposure (new product, metal, plant) and resolves with avoidance; this patient reports no new contactants and a chronic unremitting course.

key_evidence.fact: Pain worsens with activity and improves with rest
key_evidence.why: Mechanical, activity-related pain relieved by rest is characteristic of osteoarthritis, unlike the inflammatory pain of gout or rheumatoid arthritis which worsens with rest and improves with activity.

key_evidence.fact: X-rays show joint space narrowing with osteophyte formation
key_evidence.why: Joint space narrowing with osteophytes is the radiographic hallmark of osteoarthritis and distinguishes it from gout (which may show erosions with overhanging edges) and inflammatory arthritides.

key_evidence.fact: Crepitus noted in the hip during flexion and extension
key_evidence.why: Crepitus on joint motion reflects cartilage loss and is a classic physical exam finding of osteoarthritis, not typical of acute gout or septic arthritis.

key_evidence.fact: No swelling or redness over the affected joints
key_evidence.why: Lack of acute inflammatory signs argues against gout and septic arthritis, which typically present with a red, swollen, hot joint.

key_evidence.fact: Gradual progressive worsening of symptoms over several years
key_evidence.why: A chronic, slowly progressive course over years fits degenerative osteoarthritis, whereas gout attacks are acute and episodic and septic arthritis is rapidly progressive.

confusable.distinguishing: Gout causes acute, episodic attacks with a red, hot, swollen joint (often the first MTP) and elevated uric acid; here uric acid is normal (6 mg/dL) and there is no swelling or redness.

RA is inflammatory with morning stiffness improving with activity, symmetric small-joint swelling, and systemic features; this patient has mechanical pain worse with activity, no swelling, and osteophytes on X-ray.
Septic arthritis presents acutely with fever, marked joint swelling, erythema, and elevated WBC/ESR; this patient is afebrile with normal WBC and no inflammatory joint signs.

key_evidence.fact: Prolonged partial thromboplastin time (60 sec) with a normal prothrombin time (15 sec)
key_evidence.why: An isolated prolonged aPTT with normal PT localizes the defect to the intrinsic pathway, the hallmark of hemophilia, and excludes platelet and common-pathway disorders.

key_evidence.fact: Persistent bleeding after wisdom tooth extraction that is minimally responsive to gauze packs
key_evidence.why: Delayed, persistent post-procedural bleeding is characteristic of a coagulation factor deficiency rather than a platelet plug defect.

key_evidence.fact: Family history of similar bleeding and easy bruising in a maternal uncle, with joint swelling
key_evidence.why: An X-linked pattern affecting a maternal male relative with hemarthrosis strongly suggests hemophilia A or B.

key_evidence.fact: Normal platelet count (160,000/mm3) with normal-sized platelets on smear and normal bleeding time
key_evidence.why: Normal platelet number and function exclude von Willebrand disease and platelet disorders as causes of mucosal bleeding.

key_evidence.fact: History of easy bruising with old bruises of different ages on the extremities
key_evidence.why: Recurrent spontaneous bruising in a young male supports a lifelong inherited coagulopathy rather than an acquired cause.

confusable.distinguishing: vWD typically has prolonged bleeding time and often prolonged aPTT with low vWF antigen/activity; hemophilia has normal bleeding time and normal platelet function with isolated factor VIII/IX deficiency.
ITP shows thrombocytopenia with petechiae and a normal aPTT/PT; this patient has a normal platelet count and markedly prolonged aPTT.

confusable.disease: Liver disease or vitamin K deficiency
confusable.distinguishing: These prolong both PT and aPTT and may elevate bilirubin/LFTs; here PT is normal and liver chemistries are normal, pointing to an isolated intrinsic factor deficiency.

key_evidence.fact: Mucous membrane involvement with ulcers and erythema in the oropharynx (mucositis)
key_evidence.why: Mucosal involvement is a hallmark of SJS/TEN and distinguishes it from most other blistering drug eruptions and from localized contact dermatitis.

key_evidence.fact: Skin biopsy showing epidermal necrosis and detachment consistent with a severe drug reaction
key_evidence.why: Epidermal necrosis with detachment is the defining histologic feature of SJS/TEN and separates it from erythema multiforme and other mimics.

key_evidence.fact: Coalescing erythematous macules with bullae and desquamation
key_evidence.why: Progression to bullae and epidermal sloughing reflects the widespread keratinocyte death characteristic of SJS/TEN rather than a simple morbilliform drug rash.

key_evidence.fact: Recent initiation of a new medication for arthritis management (e.g., NSAID or other arthritic therapy)
key_evidence.why: A new culprit drug in the preceding weeks is the classic trigger for SJS and helps discriminate it from infection- or autoimmune-mediated blistering.

key_evidence.fact: Prodromal new-onset cough with skin and mucosal changes but no fever or systemic infection signs
key_evidence.why: A non-specific respiratory prodrome preceding mucocutaneous eruption is typical of SJS and helps distinguish it from isolated dermatologic conditions.

confusable.distinguishing: EM typically shows target lesions with limited or no mucosal involvement and lacks widespread epidermal necrosis/detachment on biopsy.
SSSS shows superficial (subcorneal) cleavage without mucosal ulceration and usually occurs in children; biopsy shows superficial epidermal split rather than full-thickness necrosis.
TEN is on the same spectrum but involves >30% body surface area detachment, whereas SJS involves <10%; the localized back involvement here favors SJS.

key_evidence.fact: The patient's mother reports that during pregnancy she had abnormal hair growth on her chin.
key_evidence.why: Maternal virilization during pregnancy is a hallmark of aromatase deficiency due to placental androgen excess, distinguishing it from other causes of delayed puberty.

key_evidence.fact: Partial labial fusion and clitoromegaly noted at birth.
key_evidence.why: Neonatal virilization in a 46,XX female indicates prenatal androgen excess, characteristic of aromatase deficiency.

key_evidence.fact: Breast development is at Tanner stage I.
key_evidence.why: Absent breast development despite normal or elevated androgens suggests impaired estrogen synthesis, as seen in aromatase deficiency.

key_evidence.fact: Height is at the 97th percentile.
key_evidence.why: Tall stature due to delayed epiphyseal closure from estrogen deficiency is typical of aromatase deficiency.

key_evidence.fact: Ovaries with multiple cysts on pelvic ultrasound.
key_evidence.why: Ovarian cysts are common in aromatase deficiency due to elevated gonadotropins and intraovarian androgen accumulation.

confusable.distinguishing: PCOS typically presents with menstrual irregularities and hyperandrogenism, but not with neonatal virilization, maternal virilization during pregnancy, or absent breast development.

CAH causes neonatal virilization but is not associated with maternal virilization during pregnancy or tall stature; it typically presents with adrenal insufficiency and specific hormone abnormalities.
AIS presents with absent breast development and primary amenorrhea, but typically with normal or tall stature and no virilization (female external genitalia); maternal virilization is not a feature.

key_evidence.fact: Fixed split S2 on inspiration
key_evidence.why: A fixed, widely split S2 that does not vary with respiration is the hallmark auscultatory finding of an ASD with left-to-right shunt, distinguishing it from innocent murmurs and other causes of a split S2.

key_evidence.fact: Echocardiogram showing an atrial septal defect with left-to-right shunt
key_evidence.why: Direct visualization of the defect with left-to-right flow confirms the diagnosis and excludes other causes of right heart volume overload.

key_evidence.fact: Enlarged cardiac silhouette on chest X-ray without pulmonary edema
key_evidence.why: Cardiomegaly reflecting right-sided volume overload without pulmonary edema supports a left-to-right shunt lesion like ASD rather than left heart failure or pneumonia.

key_evidence.fact: Mild pitting edema in both legs with hepatomegaly
key_evidence.why: Signs of right heart volume overload/failure (peripheral edema, hepatomegaly) in a child with a shunt point to a right-sided volume-loaded lesion such as ASD.

key_evidence.fact: Absence of fever, cough, or preceding illness despite rapid breathing and being unwell
key_evidence.why: Lack of infectious or respiratory symptoms makes pneumonia/bronchiolitis unlikely and shifts the differential toward a cardiac cause of tachypnea.

confusable.distinguishing: VSD typically produces a harsh pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border and a normal (not fixed) split S2; ASD has a fixed split S2 without a prominent murmur.
These present with fever, cough, and abnormal lung findings or infiltrates; this child has no fever/cough, clear lungs apart from mild rales, and cardiomegaly with an intracardiac shunt on echo.
Cardiomyopathy would show global dysfunction and often pulmonary edema; here echo demonstrates a structural ASD with left-to-right shunt and no pulmonary edema.

key_evidence.fact: Painless jaundice with pale stools and dark urine (obstructive pattern: direct bilirubin 4.8 of total 5.6, elevated ALP with normal AST/ALT)
key_evidence.why: A cholestatic (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with high ALP and normal transaminases) picture with pale stools and dark urine localizes to extrahepatic biliary obstruction, the classic presentation of a periampullary/pancreatic head tumor rather than hepatocellular disease.

key_evidence.fact: Soft, cystic mass palpated in the right upper quadrant with ultrasonography showing an anechoic cystic mass in the subhepatic region and dilated intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts
key_evidence.why: A palpable mass plus imaging evidence of a mass causing upstream biliary dilation points to a malignant obstructing lesion (e.g., pancreatic head carcinoma with a distended gallbladder/Courvoisier sign) rather than stone disease or benign stricture.

key_evidence.fact: Significant unintentional weight loss (6.3 kg) and decreased appetite over 2 weeks
key_evidence.why: Constitutional symptoms of anorexia and marked weight loss suggest malignancy and help distinguish pancreatic cancer from benign causes of biliary obstruction such as choledocholithiasis.

key_evidence.fact: Generalized pruritus accompanying the jaundice
key_evidence.why: Pruritus from bile salt accumulation is characteristic of malignant cholestasis and supports an obstructive neoplastic process over inflammatory or hepatocellular jaundice.

key_evidence.fact: 50-pack-year smoking history (and prior heavy alcohol use)
key_evidence.why: Tobacco (and chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis) are established risk factors for pancreatic adenocarcinoma, raising pretest probability when combined with obstructive jaundice and weight loss.

confusable.distinguishing: Usually presents with acute colicky RUQ pain, fever, and fluctuating jaundice; imaging shows a stone/echogenic focus rather than a solid/cystic mass, and there is typically no marked weight loss or palpable mass.

Causes pain and pancreatic calcifications/atrophy rather than a discrete obstructing mass; jaundice is less prominent and weight loss is often attributable to malabsorption, without a focal mass on ultrasound.

Also causes painless obstructive jaundice, but typically shows a bile duct stricture/mass within the duct rather than a subhepatic/pancreatic head mass; clinical overlap is high, so cross-sectional imaging and cytology are needed to localize the tumor.

key_evidence.fact: Sudden episodes of position-dependent vertigo with a false sensation of motion and spinning
key_evidence.why: Vertigo strictly provoked by changes in head position is the hallmark of BPPV and distinguishes it from spontaneous vertigo of vestibular neuritis or Meniere's disease.

key_evidence.fact: Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre positive for right-sided nystagmus when moving from sitting to supine
key_evidence.why: A positive Dix-Hallpike with characteristic positional nystagmus is the diagnostic gold standard for posterior canal BPPV and is absent in central or inflammatory causes.

key_evidence.fact: Videonystagmography shows normal vestibular response except during the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre
key_evidence.why: Preserved vestibular function outside of positional provocation excludes unilateral vestibular loss seen in vestibular neuritis and supports a canalith-displacement mechanism.

key_evidence.fact: Audiometry shows only bilateral high-frequency sensorineural loss consistent with presbycusis, with no sudden hearing drop
key_evidence.why: Absence of sudden or fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss argues against Meniere's disease and labyrinthitis, which typically accompany vertigo with auditory symptoms.

key_evidence.fact: MRI brain shows no central lesions or infarcts
key_evidence.why: Normal imaging excludes central causes of positional vertigo such as cerebellar or brainstem infarction, which can mimic BPPV.

confusable.distinguishing: Vestibular neuritis causes continuous spontaneous vertigo lasting days with unilateral vestibular hypofunction on VNG, not brief position-triggered episodes with a positive Dix-Hallpike.
Meniere's presents with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness alongside vertigo; this patient has only stable presbycusis and no auditory symptoms.
Central causes show atypical or non-fatiguing nystagmus and abnormal MRI or neurological findings; here MRI is normal and nystagmus is characteristic of BPPV.

key_evidence.fact: Presence of odd beliefs and magical thinking (belief in telepathic communication with animals)
key_evidence.why: Magical thinking and odd beliefs are core cognitive-perceptual features of schizotypal disorder that distinguish it from ordinary eccentricity or psychotic disorders with frank delusions.

key_evidence.fact: Bizarre dress (all burlap clothing)
key_evidence.why: Eccentric appearance/odd dress is a characteristic schizotypal feature reflecting social oddness, absent in most other personality disorders.

key_evidence.fact: Attempts to communicate telepathically during the interview
key_evidence.why: Observable odd/eccentric behavior in the interview setting directly demonstrates the interpersonal oddness central to schizotypal disorder.

key_evidence.fact: Lives alone and works at a health food store with social isolation
key_evidence.why: Social isolation and lack of close relationships reflect the interpersonal deficits of schizotypal disorder, helping distinguish it from schizoid (which lacks magical thinking) and from psychotic disorders.

key_evidence.fact: Poor insight and questionable judgment with self-treatment using Peruvian herbs
key_evidence.why: Odd self-treatment and impaired judgment without disorganization support a personality-level disturbance rather than an acute psychotic episode.

confusable.distinguishing: Schizoid patients show social detachment but lack magical thinking, odd beliefs, and eccentric behavior seen here.
Schizophrenia requires frank delusions/hallucinations or disorganization with functional decline; here thought process is linear and beliefs are odd rather than delusional.
Delusional disorder features a fixed, encapsulated delusion without the pervasive eccentric behavior, odd dress, and magical thinking of schizotypal disorder.

key_evidence.fact: Non-healing, red, crusty, erythematous plaque with irregular borders on the penile shaft that failed prior treatment for syphilis and eczema
key_evidence.why: A persistent, treatment-refractory erythematous crusted plaque is the classic presentation of squamous cell carcinoma in situ, distinguishing it from self-limited or treatment-responsive inflammatory and infectious mimics.

key_evidence.fact: Biopsy showing nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, and increased mitotic figures within the epithelium
key_evidence.why: These are the histologic hallmarks of carcinoma in situ (Bowen's disease), directly confirming the diagnosis and excluding benign dermatoses or infection.

key_evidence.fact: Negative syphilis serology despite prior unsuccessful syphilis treatment
key_evidence.why: Excludes syphilis, the most important infectious mimic of a penile ulcer/plaque, and explains why prior syphilis therapy failed.

key_evidence.fact: Similar lesion on the left middle finger (multiple lesions at sun-exposed and genital sites)
key_evidence.why: Multifocal lesions in Bowen's disease reflect field cancerization and support in-situ neoplastic disease rather than a single localized infection or eczema.

key_evidence.fact: History of chronic heavy smoking (2 packs/day for 30 years)
key_evidence.why: Tobacco is a recognized risk factor for Bowen's disease and penile squamous neoplasia, raising pretest probability and discriminating from purely infectious or eczematous causes.

confusable.distinguishing: Syphilis serology is negative and lesions failed appropriate syphilis treatment; syphilitic lesions are typically transient and treatment-responsive, unlike the persistent plaque with malignant histology.
Inflammatory dermatoses respond to topical steroids and lack cytologic atypia (hyperchromasia, multinucleation, mitoses) on biopsy; this lesion was treatment-refractory and histologically malignant.
Invasive SCC shows dermal invasion beyond the basement membrane; Bowen's disease is confined to the epithelium (carcinoma in situ) without invasive nests.

key_evidence.fact: He often refuses to participate in directed activities with responses such as 'You're not the boss of me' or 'You can't make me.'
key_evidence.why: Persistent argumentativeness and active defiance toward adults is the core symptom of ODD and distinguishes it from mere noncompliance or inattention.

key_evidence.fact: He is reluctant to participate in gym class, though he engages actively in similar physical activities during recess.
key_evidence.why: Refusal limited to adult-directed settings while engaging in the same activity freely points to oppositional defiance rather than a motor or anxiety-related avoidance.

key_evidence.fact: His social interactions with peers are positive, and he is described as well-liked by his classmates.
key_evidence.why: Preserved peer relationships argue against conduct disorder and autism spectrum disorder, where peer conflict or social deficits are typical.

key_evidence.fact: The patient's mother describes him as occasionally difficult but notes that he is helpful at home and plays well with his younger sister.
key_evidence.why: Behavior largely confined to school with cooperative home behavior suggests ODD rather than a pervasive conduct or mood disorder.

key_evidence.fact: Parent and teacher behavioral checklists indicate patterns consistent with oppositional behaviors without conduct problems, and psychological evaluation shows no anxiety, depression, or ADHD.
key_evidence.why: Objective rating scales confirming oppositionality without conduct, mood, or attention pathology specifically support ODD over its mimics.

confusable.distinguishing: Conduct disorder involves violation of others' rights (aggression, theft, destruction, deceit), which is absent here; this child is well-liked and has no conduct problems on checklists.
ADHD would show pervasive inattention/hyperactivity across settings and impair peer relations; here psychological evaluation is negative for ADHD and behavior is defiance-specific.
ASD would show social communication deficits and rigid routines; this child has positive peer relationships and no social deficits.

key_evidence.fact: Painless jaundice with an enlarged, non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) on palpation and ultrasound
key_evidence.why: A palpable, non-tender distended gallbladder in the setting of jaundice strongly suggests malignant distal biliary obstruction rather than stone disease, which typically produces a tender or non-distended gallbladder.

key_evidence.fact: Significantly elevated ALP with elevated bilirubin and only modest transaminase elevation
key_evidence.why: A cholestatic enzyme pattern points to biliary obstruction, and the disproportionate ALP rise discriminates malignant obstruction from hepatocellular causes of jaundice.

key_evidence.fact: Unintentional weight loss over the last month despite dietary changes
key_evidence.why: Constitutional weight loss with jaundice raises suspicion for a malignancy such as pancreatic cancer rather than benign biliary obstruction.

key_evidence.fact: Ultrasound showing an enlarged, thin-walled gallbladder with no evident stones
key_evidence.why: Absence of stones with a dilated gallbladder supports obstruction distal to the cystic duct, typical of a pancreatic head tumor rather than cholelithiasis.

key_evidence.fact: Heavy smoking (1 pack/day) and daily alcohol use in a 65-year-old
key_evidence.why: Tobacco and alcohol exposure are established risk factors for pancreatic adenocarcinoma, increasing pretest probability when cholestatic jaundice is present.

confusable.distinguishing: Usually presents with colicky abdominal pain and a tender gallbladder; stones are seen on ultrasound, whereas this case has painless jaundice and no stones.

Also causes painless cholestatic jaundice, but typically does not produce a markedly enlarged, palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) unless the obstruction is distal; imaging showing a pancreatic head mass favors pancreatic cancer.
Often has a history of recurrent abdominal pain and calcifications or ductal changes on imaging; painless progressive jaundice with weight loss and a dilated gallbladder favors malignancy.

key_evidence.fact: Toxicology screen positive for amphetamines with negative cocaine, opiates, benzodiazepines, and cannabinoids
key_evidence.why: A positive amphetamine screen with negative cocaine isolates a sympathomimetic stimulant as the cause, distinguishing it from cocaine or mixed intoxications.

key_evidence.fact: Dilated pupils, diaphoresis, tachycardia (120/min), and temperature 101°F in an agitated young man
key_evidence.why: This constellation is the classic sympathomimetic toxidrome of amphetamine intoxication, discriminating it from anticholinergic or serotonin syndromes.

key_evidence.fact: Rapid speech, extreme irritability, aggression, and breaking objects after prolonged stress
key_evidence.why: Acute agitation with pressured speech and aggression reflects amphetamine-induced CNS stimulation, distinguishing it from primary psychiatric mania or psychosis.

key_evidence.fact: Prolonged physical activity (several hours at the gym) despite exhaustion
key_evidence.why: Sustained hyperactivity and endurance beyond normal limits is characteristic of stimulant intoxication and helps separate it from depressive or anxiety disorders.

key_evidence.fact: Absence of fever, vomiting, diarrhea, dysuria, or flank pain before the event, with normal WBC and chemistry panel
key_evidence.why: Normal inflammatory and metabolic labs exclude infection, sepsis, or metabolic encephalopathy as causes of the agitation and tachycardia.

confusable.distinguishing: Cocaine would produce a positive cocaine screen and typically shorter duration; here amphetamines are positive and cocaine negative.
Primary psychiatric illness lacks the sympathomimetic toxidrome (dilated pupils, diaphoresis, fever, tachycardia) and a positive amphetamine screen.
Anticholinergic toxicity shows dry skin and flushing rather than diaphoresis, and serotonin syndrome shows clonus/hyperreflexia; neither has a positive amphetamine screen.

key_evidence.fact: Cervical motion tenderness present on pelvic examination
key_evidence.why: Cervical motion tenderness is a cardinal criterion for PID and helps distinguish it from appendicitis or simple UTI, which do not produce this finding.

key_evidence.fact: Purulent cervical discharge noted on pelvic examination
key_evidence.why: Mucopurulent cervical discharge reflects ascending genital tract infection and is a key PID criterion, distinguishing it from non-infectious causes of pelvic pain.

key_evidence.fact: Burning pain during sexual intercourse (dyspareunia) reported 3 days ago
key_evidence.why: Dyspareunia from inflamed pelvic organs supports PID and is less typical of appendicitis or uncomplicated cystitis.

key_evidence.fact: Sexually active with inconsistent condom use
key_evidence.why: Inconsistent barrier protection is a major risk factor for sexually transmitted ascending infection, strongly favoring PID over other acute abdominal conditions.

key_evidence.fact: Temperature 38.5°C with leukocytosis (15,000/mm3) and ESR 100 mm/h
key_evidence.why: Systemic inflammatory markers with fever indicate an active pelvic infection, supporting PID and arguing against functional or non-inflammatory causes of pelvic pain.

confusable.distinguishing: Appendicitis typically causes migratory right lower quadrant pain with McBurney point tenderness and lacks cervical motion tenderness or purulent cervical discharge.
Cystitis causes dysuria and frequency without cervical motion tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, or high ESR; this patient denies frequency and urgency.
Ectopic pregnancy presents with amenorrhea, positive pregnancy test, and unilateral adnexal findings; PID has cervical motion tenderness and purulent discharge with a negative pregnancy test.
